## Demo 

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/acc25ad9-d295-487b-8c93-e0034d8eb40e

## Before

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/70ae28a3-62c9-4be2-b082-d4670ad509de

## After

https://github.com/user-attachments/assets/21d91579-619f-4520-93c3-4021c2576eee

Adds an opt-in option to Agent Host automations, **Same Chat**. When it's on, each run sends the automation's prompt in the chat of the automation's latest run instead of creating a new chat, so a recurring automation keeps its conversation. It's off by default.

In the automation dialog it's a switch next to **Run in the Cloud**, and hovering it explains what it does. Cloud runs can't continue a chat, so while Run in the Cloud is on, the switch is off and disabled with the reason "Not available in the cloud"; turning the cloud off brings back your choice. The `configureAutomation` tool takes the same option as `continueSession`.

**How it works** (the code calls a chat a session)

- The option is stored in the definition's `_meta` (`vscode.automationContinueSession`), and the host advertises a capability with the same name. The dialog and the tool offer the option only when the host supports it. No protocol change.
- Each run still gets its own run entry. The host links the previous run's session to the new run without a creation journal, so restart recovery never deletes it.
- If the session is running a turn (such as the user's), or an earlier run that ran a turn there hasn't ended (even while it waits to resume after a wake), the run waits and then starts its turn, in the order runs are due. Its message is tagged with the run (`vscode.automationRun`), so the run ends only with its own turn. Cancelling a waiting run ends it without touching the session's turn. A run whose session was archived while it waited fails. While a run waits or creates its session, further due occurrences are skipped, as they would only repeat its prompt.
- Before the run's turn starts, the session gets the automation's current customizations as its `vscode.automation` active client, because a restored session has no active clients and the automation's plugins may have changed since the session was created.
- A run creates a new session, which later runs continue, when the previous session is gone, archived, or from another provider, or when the automation's provider, folders or persistent configuration (such as mode, approvals, sandbox, isolation and branch, including a provider's own settings like Codex approvals) changed since that session was created, or its model was cleared (a turn without a model keeps its session's). The host records the time of such an edit on the entry's `_meta` (`vscode.sessionTemplateChangedAt`), and each run records the value its session was created from, so a run that was due before an edit but created its session after it is still continued. Archiving or deleting the session starts over.
- History shows a session shared by several runs once, for its newest run.
- `src/vs/sessions/AUTOMATIONS.md` describes the new run lifecycle.

## How to test

1. In the Agents window, create an automation with the **Manual** trigger and the prompt "Reply with just one number: the next number after the last number you said in this conversation. If you have not said a number yet, reply 1. Do not use any tools."
2. Edit it, turn on **Same Chat**, and save.
3. Run it twice. Both runs use one chat, and the replies are 1, then 2. History lists that chat once.
4. In that chat, send a message, and run the automation while the reply is still running. The run waits for your turn, then replies 3.
5. Click **New Automation** and turn on **Run in the Cloud**: Same Chat turns off and says "Not available in the cloud". Turn the cloud off again: Same Chat is back as you left it.

The new tests fail without the change.

- Checked live in a Code OSS build of this branch (the videos above), including the waiting run from step 4 and the cloud state from step 5.

Scenarios.Scenario: An opted-in scheduled or manual automation continues the latest run's chat when that session is currently unloaded
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Run dispatch scans retained run metadata to select the latest session, validates it through the host database, restores the session and its default chat/history, persists the running/link lifecycle, then starts the provider turn. The database, restore, chat-history load, storage writes, and provider send are on the run's critical path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Read the candidate session registration and list provisional-session markers.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One targeted registration query plus one provisional-list query for the single latest candidate per opted-in run.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Every run skipped these validation reads and proceeded to allocate/create a new session.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Both queries must complete before deciding whether to reuse or create a session.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Restore an evicted session and resolve its default chat history from provider/session storage.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: At most one cold session restore and one cold chat-history resolution for the selected session; repeated restore calls join or take the resident fast path.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: A fresh empty session was created, so no previous chat history was restored; session creation had its own provider and storage cost.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Cold restore/history resolution blocks starting the continued turn.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist automation run lifecycle/link state including retained run state.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: Two existing-style durable state writes per started run; the continued path does not add a third write.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Fresh-session runs also persisted running and linked states in two writes.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Both durable mutations precede provider turn start.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send the automation prompt as a provider turn in the restored chat.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One provider turn per non-coalesced run.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: One provider turn was sent in a newly created chat instead of the prior chat.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: This is the principal run execution boundary after admission.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: One candidate session per run after selecting the latest prior run; selection scales with retained automation-run history, while restored chat data scales with the shared conversation's turn history. The effective run history is retained beyond the 50-item presentation window, but existing persistence and run-window construction already process that history.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Run-state mutations remain globally sequenced by the existing mutation queue. Continued starts are serialized per session with ThrottlerByKey; different sessions can proceed independently. A schedule coalesces additional due occurrences while one continued run has not started.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: A resident session makes the second restore and chat resolution fast-path state checks; an evicted session performs a cold provider/storage restore and loads chat history. There is no negative cache for a missing/archived candidate, but the failed candidate causes a new session whose run becomes the next candidate rather than repeated retries against the old session.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence in the exact database, restore, persistence, and provider call path; uncertain provider-specific cost does not change the traced cardinality.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Provider restore and shared-history costs vary by provider, eviction, and conversation length. The feature is opt-in and these costs are intrinsic to preserving chat context; the diff also avoids fresh session allocation/creation, so no independent actionable regression is established.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding. The new boundaries occur only for the opted-in reuse behavior and replace fresh-session allocation/creation; calls are one-candidate, serialized, and cold work is cached by resident session/chat state.

Scenarios.Scenario: A continued automation becomes due while its shared chat is running a user turn or an earlier automation turn
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The run validates and links the shared session, makes one start attempt, then waits event-driven. A terminal chat action schedules the next per-session attempt, which restores/resolves through warm state and starts the turn. No timer polling or repeated boundary loop blocks the existing user turn.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Restore/resolve the shared session and chat before checking admission.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One attempt when linked and one event-triggered attempt when the blocking turn ends; no polling with wait duration.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Runs created independent sessions and did not wait on another turn in a shared chat.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The first attempt establishes that the run must wait; the later attempt is on the continued run's start path, not the blocking user's turn path.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Persist link, cancellation, and terminal lifecycle transitions.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One write per state transition; cancellation holds the waiter so persistence cannot race an additional start.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: Equivalent run lifecycle transitions were already durably persisted, though there was no shared-session waiter.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: Link persistence precedes start; cancellation persistence prevents the waiting run from starting.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Waiting work scales with the number of distinct shared sessions, not elapsed wait time. Additional due occurrences for the same automation are skipped while a run is creating or waiting, and only the earliest waiting run for a session is selected.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: ThrottlerByKey permits one active start attempt per session and coalesces requests arriving during it. Existing mutation serialization orders durable links/cancellation; separate sessions remain independent.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: The initial validation usually makes the session resident. Retries after turn completion use warm session and chat state unless residency evicted the session during a long wait; per-session throttling prevents duplicate concurrent restores.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence from the per-session throttler, continued-run map, turn terminal event path, and schedule coalescing condition.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Very long user turns and provider-specific eviction can make the eventual warm/cold distinction vary, but attempt count remains bounded and event-driven.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding. The diff explicitly coalesces due occurrences and serializes starts per session, avoiding polling, duplicate turns, and a concurrency burst.

Scenarios.Scenario: Automation scheduling with multiple definitions and retained run history
Scenarios.CriticalPath: At each earliest schedule wake, the scheduler walks available definitions. For definitions using Same Chat it scans retained runs to detect an already waiting/unlinked run, then advances cursors and performs the existing durable catalog/run write when state changes.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Serialize and flush the automation catalog and all retained runs after schedule cursor/run changes.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One flush for a schedule-claim batch, as before; no per-definition flush.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same full retained-run state was flushed for schedule claims.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The batch flush completes before claimed state is published and runs start.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: The new waiting-run check is O(total retained runs) per Same Chat definition examined at a schedule wake; retained runs are unbounded by the 50-item presentation window. However existing claimed-run summary construction sorts retained runs and existing persistence serializes all retained runs on each claimed occurrence, which already dominates long-history schedules.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Schedule claiming is globally sequenced through the mutation queue and creates at most one run per automation per tick; subsequent starts may run independently by session after the claim.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Run state is in-memory; there is no separate active-run index. Durable storage is rewritten through the existing storage service after changed schedule state.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence in the O(definitions × retained runs) check and existing larger costs; low evidence that the increment creates a user-visible regression.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: The number of long-lived high-frequency automations is unknown, but the added in-memory scan is not independently material relative to unchanged full-history summary sorting and durable serialization on the same due-run path.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding. Although the diff adds a history scan for Same Chat definitions, it prevents duplicate waiting runs and is not shown to materially amplify the already history-scaling claim/persistence path.

Scenarios.Scenario: Open/edit an automation dialog or configure it through the automation tool
Scenarios.CriticalPath: The UI reads provider capability from in-memory provider/store state, renders one additional switch, and includes one metadata boolean in the existing create/update operation. Tool validation similarly performs an in-memory capability check before the existing operation.

ExpensiveBoundaries.Operation: Send the existing automation create/update request with the continue-session metadata flag.
ExpensiveBoundaries.Cardinality: One existing request per user save or accepted tool operation; payload grows by one boolean metadata property.
ExpensiveBoundaries.PreviousBehavior: The same create/update request was sent without this metadata property.
ExpensiveBoundaries.CriticalPathEffect: The existing request remains on save/configure's critical path.

Scenarios.ScalingInput: Constant work per dialog render/change and per configure invocation; customization collections and provider count are unchanged.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: No new parallel work, queue, subprocess, or fan-out. The save/configure operation retains the provider store's existing sequencing.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: Capability state comes from the current connected store/initialize result; no new cache or repeated remote lookup is introduced.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence from the dialog, tool, provider service, and store call paths.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: None material; DOM and metadata additions are constant-sized.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding. The UI and tool changes add constant in-memory/DOM work and no additional boundary call.

Scenarios.Scenario: Render automation run history when several runs share one session
Scenarios.CriticalPath: Each history render filters the already supplied run array using a Set of session object identities, then performs the existing grouping/list rendering. Focus restoration may scan the current focus-target collection only when focus was owned by history.
Scenarios.ScalingInput: Linear in loaded run rows and focus targets. Effective cardinality is the currently loaded/paged history, and duplicate shared sessions reduce downstream rows and DOM work.
Scenarios.EffectiveConcurrency: Synchronous UI rendering on the existing render call; no async fan-out or boundary concurrency.
Scenarios.CacheBehavior: No cache is introduced; a short-lived Set is allocated per render and released. Session data is supplied by existing observable/service caches.
Scenarios.MechanismConfidence: High confidence from the changed render method and history paging model.
Scenarios.MagnitudeUncertainty: Loaded history can be paged beyond 50, but the new linear filter replaces rendering duplicate rows, so net DOM/layout work decreases for shared sessions.
Scenarios.Verdict: No finding. The added linear filter is bounded by loaded history and avoids more expensive duplicate session-row rendering.

Analysis.Summary: Completed the performance pass over all 22 changed files and the full paginated diff. Traced continued-run admission, scheduler behavior, session/database/filesystem/provider boundaries, UI/tool configuration, and history rendering. No high-confidence actionable performance regression was introduced; the opt-in cold restore/history costs replace new-session creation, waiting work is coalesced and per-session serialized, and UI work is constant or reduces rendered rows.
